newsitem.title: ZAIRE: U.S. envoy says Zaire's Mobutu, Kabila to meet.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy says Zaire's Mobutu, Kabila to meet.

text.p: U.S. troubleshooter Bill Richardson said on Tuesday Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila and President Mobutu Sese Seko had agreed to their first face-to-face meeting.

Richardson, who met Mobutu in Kinshasa before flying to rebel-held Lubumbashi for talks with Kabila, referred to the latter as "president" -- apparently to drive home the U.S. position that Mobuto should step down.

"The objective of President (Bill) Clinton sending me here is to have face-to-face talks between President Mobutu and President Kabila," Richardson, U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, told reporters on arrival in Lubumbashi.

"I am happy that both men have agreed to meet. But I will be working out other details with Mr Kabila on free and fair elections, the rule of law which should follow after the end of the war in Zaire."

But Kabila told Reuters shortly before he started talks with Richardson that elections could only be held after Mobutu had stepped down or was overthrown and even then the president and "his corrupt entourage cannot take part in such a process".

"There will be no compromise over the departure, through the battlefield or at talks of Mobutu, his system and his henchmen," he said. "Mobutu and everything he represents must go before we can think of holding elections."
Kabila said rebels were advancing by road to Zaire's capital after capturing Kikwit town on Tuesday. "We have advanced beyond Kikwit. Our destination is Kinshasa," the rebel leader said.
Rebels entered Kikwit, 400 km (250 miles) from Kinshasa, on Tuesday and were greeted by crowds of jubilant residents. Kabila said that his fighters had also taken the town's large airport.
Richardson said he had a "very fruitful" meeting with Mobutu earlier on Tuesday in Kinshasa and suggested that a good goal for the first meeting between both men would be this weekend.
"I have agreed to (South African) President (Nelson) Mandela's request that I meet Mr Mobutu on a ship off the Atlantic coastline to discuss Mr Mobutu's departure," Kabila said.
"As far as I am concerned this will be a short ceremony at which Mr Mobutu is supposed to agree to leave, otherwise our forces now advancing on the route to Kinshasa will eject him.
"I am made to believe he (Mobutu) will cooperate with us and avoid a bloody confrontation for Kinshasa," Kabila added.

Asked about when, Kabila said it would be in the next few days and Mandela and U.N. envoy Mohamed Sahnoun were working on an agreeable date but the most important thing was that both men had agreed to meet.
South Africa said on Tuesday it hoped to host the face-to-face talks between Mobutu and Kabila before the weekend -- on a former Russian naval ship dubbed the "Grey Diplomat".
"We hope that the talks will take place before the weekend," Deputy Foreign Affairs Minister Aziz Pahad told reporters.
Mobutu, who has cancer, ruled out South Africa as too far on health grounds. Kabila ruled out Congo's capital Brazzaville, over the river from Kinshasa, and Gabon on security grounds.
A senior rebel commander said in Lubumbashi that Mobutu's Presidential Guard had strongly defended Kikwit airport, which rebels needed as a springboard for a final assault on Kinshasa.
Richardson plans to visit Zaire's rebel-held third city of Kisangani on Wednesday and possibly Angola, which Kinshasa has accused of invading Zaire to back the Tutsi-dominated rebels.
The rebels, fighting since October, control over half of Zaire, Africa's third largest nation at the continent's heart.
Richardson's trip to Kisangani will focus on the plight of thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees and displaced Zaireans. Kabila has given aid agencies 60 days to repatriate them all.
The agencies said they had increasingly shocking reports of killings of Hutu refugees both around Kisangani and elsewhere.
The Hutu refugees fled Rwanda in 1994 and are collectively accused by minority Tutsis of genocide in Rwanda the same year.
